summary: The study compares the growth of ZnS thin films on a rough ceramic substrate using vacuum deposition, electron-beam evaporation, and atomic layer epitaxy (ALE). It highlights that ALE provides uniform and complete coverage, unlike the shadowing effect observed in vacuum and electron-beam methods. The ALE process uses DMZ and H2S as precursors and operates at 200 °C. The results show that ALE is advantageous for thin film electroluminescent devices on rough substrates.
evidence: The results clearly show a non-uniform and incomplete coverage of the substrate in the case of films grown by electron-beam evaporation and resistance-heated evaporation. A shadowing effect is observed in these films. On the contrary, films grown by the atomic layer epitaxy method, exhibit a complete and uniform coverage of the substrate, even for thin (<100nm) ZnS films. The ALE system, operating at atmospheric pressure, uses dimethylzinc (DMZ) and hydrogen sulphide (H2S) as reactants. It is known that the substrate temperature is extremely critical in thin-film growth of ZnS. For the sake of comparison, the substrate temperature was identical (200°C) for all the samples investigated. The third method of deposition used was atmospheric pressure atomic layer epitaxy. Use is made of the reaction between the two gaseous reactants, DMZ and H2S, to give ZnS.
